patch.objective: Recognize postpartum hemorrhage as blood loss of 1,000 mL or more within 24 hours, and report heavy bleeding at once

sources.note: Relayed from the LPN/VN course's earlier cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read for this band: the practical nursing course is built toward this test plan.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

Relayed from the NCLEX-PN case postpartum-check-boggy-fundus, not re-read for this band; its note: Relayed from the REQ-240 LPN/VN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: 'Recognize and report change in client condition'; the course seed tags the postpartum objective to page 13 of this plan (health promotion: care of the client in the postpartum period).

Relayed from the NCLEX-PN case postpartum-check-boggy-fundus, not re-read for this band; its note: Read directly 2026-11-16 on openstax.org (sections 20.1, 20.3 and 21.2, web pages, through a summarizing fetch that returned quotes); every value used here matches. 20.1: 'A full bladder can also cause the uterus to be boggy, rise above the umbilicus, and be deviated to one side'; 'If the fundus is boggy, the nurse massages the fundus'; 'A temperature above 100.4º F (38º C) is not expected'; a client who cannot empty the bladder is catheterized per the postpartum orders. 20.3: report 'heavy, bright red blood or clots saturating more than one pad in an hour'. 21.2: PPH is '1,000 mL of blood loss within 24 hours of birth for both vaginal and cesarean births' (ACOG 2017), atony the most common cause of early PPH; 'classic signs of hypovolemia may not occur until a significant hemorrhage has occurred.'

Relayed from the NCLEX-PN case postpartum-check-boggy-fundus, not re-read for this band; its note: Read directly again 2026-11-16 (summarizing fetch with quotes; the page shows no authors or update date; the NCBI Bookshelf edition NBK499988, Wormer, Jamil and Bryant, updated 2024-07-19, says the same): cumulative blood loss over 1000 mL, or blood loss with signs of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth; uterine atony is the most common cause; tachycardia and hypotension may be masked in postpartum women, so a large loss can sit behind normal vital signs.
